I've mixed my opinion with some of the author's (s/he's quoted below).

TPP isn't really about "free trade" because we had free trade with most of the world since the 1970s. TPP is about coordinating laws across borders. In principle coordinating can be good or bad:

  • A good example is if every country on earth entered into a treaty to drive on the left or on the right. This would save everyone money because then auto manufacturers wouldn't have to make two models of the same car.
  • A bad example is if auto emissions requirements were standardized at the lowest level. If you've ever seen what Beijing air looks like, you might not want it. (Note: China's new passenger car laws are now on par with the EU, but historically not).

Here is the problem (below direct from author)

One of the worst parts of the leaked drafts involves investor-state dispute settlement. This started out as a way for Western companies to do business safely in tinpot Third World countries--if some dictator decided to expropriate their property, they could sue in an extraterritorial court. But now First World governments are being treated on the same terms.

The most notorious example is Australia, which passed a law saying that cigs had to use plain packaging. This was a very good law--people who want cigs can still buy them, but people who are actually buying the cool marketing images can go buy something else with cool images that also won't kill them as quickly. And as it happens, cig sales have gone down. Australia got sued by Philip Morris, even though this was no interference with free trade (that is, it applied to foreign and domestic companies equally). The case is still pending, but the point is that the decision will be made by the WTO, not by Australians, and that Australians had no idea that they were agreeing to any such thing when they signed a "free trade" treaty (with Hong Kong, no less, where Philip Morris has a subsidiary). The TPP looks to be making it much easier for companies to sue when states pass laws they don't like.

Since only multinational companies have the power to use these extra-national "courts" -- we can assume they will use them to fight to apply the weakest laws in countries that currently have strong laws. And it won't be easy to stop them because citizens don't have a voice in these courts.

Another example -- the U.S. has crazy-strong copyright infringement laws (jail time) and endless protection-terms. The RIAA would love to see these applied in places like Vietnam (in the TPP).

Obama claims TPP will be awesome, because we'll spread U.S. laws everywhere else (U.S. guns in Australia anyone?), but the more rational (cynical) observer anticipates that the most consumer-unfriendly laws are what will be spread into the U.S.
